::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Effects on pupil size are often attributed to the noradrenergic locus coeruleus, without acknowledging other neuromodulators.
We quantify the extent of this bias in the literature.
Strikingly, more than half of the articles on pupil-linked arousal in humans focus primarily on noradrenaline and fail to mention other neuromodulators while interpreting results.
Over recent years, pupil size under constant luminance has become a valuable biomarker of arousal.
While basic pupillary reflexes are well-characterized, the neural systems underlying arousal-related pupil dynamics remain an area of ongoing research.
Early work in rhesus monkeys identified the locus coeruleus, a brainstem nucleus that serves as the brain's main source of noradrenaline, as a key driver of pupil-linked arousal [1, 2].

text.text: We observed a widespread noradrenaline-centric bias in studies that use pupil size as a proxy for arousal: researchers frequently ascribe their findings to the noradrenergic locus coeruleus while giving little or no attention to other neuromodulators.
To evaluate this impression, here we quantified the extent of the noradrenaline-centric bias in the literature.

We conducted a systematic survey of the literature on pupil-linked arousal (see Table 1 and its legend for Methods), including all empirical papers on pupil size and arousal published from 2017 onward.

text.text: One limitation of our method is that statements such as "pupil size reflects activity of brainstem arousal systems, such as the noradrenergic system" (paraphrased rather than quoted, as our aim is not to single out individual studies) are coded as mentioning noradrenaline but no other neuromodulators, even though they are relatively nuanced and consistent with current evidence.
To gauge the impact of this limitation, we manually surveyed all human studies from 2024 onwards that mentioned noradrenaline and not any other neuromodulators according to our analysis.

Seven out of 76 papers (9%) explicitly acknowledged these nuances, for example by noting that the pupil-noradrenaline relationship is not fully defined or that multiple arousal systems contribute to pupil dilation (without specifying these).
The remaining 91% of papers initially classified as noradrenaline-centric indeed made overly reductive claims.
Overall, our analysis reveals a strong noradrenaline-centric bias in the interpretation of pupillinked arousal, particularly in human neuroscience.

The reduction to a single neurochemical system is not merely a matter of wording; it shapes how neurobiological mechanisms are inferred from pupillometry and hinders theoretical progress on arousal-cognition relationships.
By neglecting the roles of other neuromodulators, the field risks drawing incomplete or misleading conclusions about the neural processes that support cognition and behavior.
Recognizing and integrating the diversity of neuromodulatory influences on pupil size is therefore crucial.
